subject: history
title: Reconstruction, the Gilded Age and Progressivism
welcome_lead: From Appomattox to Theodore Roosevelt: rebuilding the Union and reforming industrial America.
meta_desc: AQA A-Level USA adventure on Reconstruction 1865-77, the Gilded Age and Progressive Era reforms.
final_note: You can assess how far Reconstruction and Progressivism delivered lasting change.

concepts.def: Post-Civil War effort to readmit Southern states and protect freedpeople; ended by the Compromise of 1877.
Reconstruction Amendments (1865, 1868, 1870) abolishing slavery, granting birthright citizenship and equal protection, and prohibiting racial barriers to the vote.
System of state-level segregation laws emerging in the South from the 1880s, validated by Plessy v Ferguson 1896.
Term coined by Mark Twain for c.1870-1900: rapid industrialisation, immigration, urbanisation, political corruption.
First federal statute against trusts and monopolies, weakly enforced until Theodore Roosevelt's 'trust-busting'.
c.1890-1920 reform movement targeting corporate power, corruption and social ills; key figures Theodore Roosevelt, Wilson; muckrakers like Sinclair.

walkthroughs.body_html: Lincoln's assassination on 14 April 1865 left Andrew Johnson confronting Radical Republicans. Congressional Reconstruction (Acts of 1867) divided the South into military districts. The Freedmen's Bureau (1865-72) supported education. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) prohibited racial voting barriers. White paramilitary terror (Ku Klux Klan founded 1865) and Northern fatigue led to the Compromise of 1877: federal troops withdrew, ending Reconstruction.

Carnegie steel, Rockefeller's Standard Oil and Vanderbilt railroads symbolised concentrated wealth. Approximately 25 million immigrants arrived 1870-1914. Political machines (Tammany Hall) and patronage dominated. The People's (Populist) Party challenged the gold standard; Bryan lost the 1896 election to McKinley. Plessy v Ferguson (1896) legitimised 'separate but equal'.

Theodore Roosevelt's 'Square Deal' (1901-09) pursued trust-busting (Northern Securities 1904), the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) and Hepburn Act (1906). Taft continued antitrust action. Wilson's 'New Freedom' delivered the Underwood Tariff (1913), the Federal Reserve Act (1913), the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) and the 16th-19th Amendments (1913-20: income tax, direct election of senators, Prohibition, women's suffrage).
